subject: general
question: Which Indian judgment laid down the concept of ‘Basic Structure’ of the Constitution?

options.text: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
Minerva Mills v. Union of India
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India

solution:
The correct answer is __**Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The concept of the **‘Basic Structure’** of the Constitution was first propounded in the landmark case of **Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)**. This judgment is considered one of the most significant in Indian constitutional history.
 
• The Supreme Court ruled that while the Parliament has vast powers under **Article 368** of the Indian Constitution to amend the Constitution, it cannot alter or destroy its **basic structure**.
 
• The judgment introduced the doctrine that certain fundamental features of the Constitution, such as **democracy, rule of law, separation of powers, and judicial review**, are inviolable and cannot be amended.
 
• The case arose when the Kerala government passed laws to regulate land ownership and impose land reforms, which were challenged by the petitioner, Kesavananda Bharati, on the grounds that they violated his fundamental rights.
 
• This judgment limited the Parliament's power to amend the Constitution and protected the spirit of the Indian Constitution from being eroded by arbitrary amendments.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Other Landmark Cases Related to Constitutional Amendments:**

 
 
• **Golaknath v. State of Punjab (1967):** The Supreme Court ruled that **Parliament cannot amend fundamental rights**. This decision was later overturned in the Kesavananda Bharati case.
 
• **Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980):** This case reaffirmed the doctrine of the basic structure and held that a balance between **Fundamental Rights** and **Directive Principles** is part of the Constitution's basic structure.
 
• **Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978):** This case expanded the interpretation of **Article 21**, emphasizing that the right to life and personal liberty cannot be curtailed except by a procedure that is fair, just, and reasonable.
 
 
 
• **Basic Structure Doctrine:**
 
 
• Examples of elements within the **basic structure** include **sovereignty, secularism, federalism, separation of powers, and judicial independence**.
 
• The doctrine ensures that constitutional amendments cannot alter the essence of the Constitution, preserving its core values and framework.
 
 
 
• **Impact of Kesavananda Bharati Case:**
 
 
• It introduced a mechanism for judicial review of constitutional amendments to ensure they align with the Constitution's basic structure.
 
• It marked a turning point in Indian constitutional law, emphasizing the supremacy of the Constitution over parliamentary authority.
 
• This case is often regarded as the **‘savior of the Constitution’**, ensuring the protection of fundamental rights and democratic principles.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Article 368:**
 
 
• Article 368 provides the **power to amend the Constitution**, but the Kesavananda Bharati judgment clarified that this power is not absolute and is subject to judicial review.
 
• The article plays a critical role in maintaining the Constitution's flexibility while ensuring its core principles are preserved.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Parliamentary Authority vs. Judicial Review:**

 
 
• The Kesavananda Bharati judgment struck a balance between the **amending power of Parliament** and the **judicial review power of the judiciary**.
 
• The ruling emphasized that neither Parliament nor the judiciary is supreme, but the **Constitution is the ultimate authority**.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Judicial Independence:**
 
 
• The judgment reinforced the independence of the judiciary as a guardian of the Constitution, ensuring checks and balances in governance.
 
• This independence is critical for upholding the rule of law and protecting the rights of citizens.
